rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Though the Resurrection is a universal judgment, every person experiences utter aloneness.
rows.anchor: although the Day of Resurrection is a day of universal judgment, every person will feel utterly alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People return alone as they were first created, and naked, wholly dependent on God.
rows.anchor: that is, alone (see 74:11c) and naked (JJ)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Judgment comes without worldly means, wealth, associates, or children that had provided status and protection; these goods are left behind.
rows.anchor: without the benefit of their worldly means, wealth, associates, and children (Z)

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī
rows.claim: Worldly goods and the bond to them are left behind, but knowledge of God, virtue, and good deeds are sent ahead and met with greater reward.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī explains that, although worldly goods are left behind and that the connection between these goods and the one who strove to acquire them is severed

words: شُفَعَآءَكُمُ ٱلَّذِينَ زَعَمْتُمْ أَنَّهُمْ فِيكُمْ شُرَكَٰٓؤُا۟
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The supposed intercessors are false idols or deities claimed as God's partners and credited with power to intercede.
rows.anchor: Your intercessors here refers to the false idols or deities they had ascribed as partners unto God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran repeatedly depicts false idols, deities, authorities, and Satan disowning or forsaking their earthly followers.
rows.anchor: false idols, deities, and authorities, including Satan, will disown and “forsake” those who followed or venerated them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qisṭ means justice, and here answers the disbelievers' allegation that God commands indecency; it can also mean what is right or proper.
rows.anchor: not indecency, as the disbelievers allege in v. 28.

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some connect qisṭ with the testimony of faith, following the verse where God and knowledgeable witnesses uphold justice.
rows.anchor: connected by some with the testimony of faith, “There is no god but God,” following 3:18

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Setting one's face means facing the qiblah toward the Sacred Mosque in Makkah.
rows.anchor: toward the qiblah, or direction of prayer, which is toward the Sacred Mosque in Makkah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One possible reading is to face the qiblah at every place one prays, wherever one may be.
rows.anchor: turn toward the qiblah in prayer “wheresoever you may be”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another possible reading is to face the qiblah at every prayer time.
rows.anchor: the verse could also mean to turn toward the qiblah at every time of prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning or submitting one's face to God is a Quranic image for orienting one's whole being toward worship and obedience.
rows.anchor: signifying the orientation of one’s whole being toward worship of and obedience to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling upon God most commonly means supplicating Him for spiritual and material needs.
rows.anchor: To call upon Him most commonly means to supplicate God for one’s spiritual and material needs

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators instead take calling upon God here to mean canonical prayer or worship generally.
rows.anchor: some commentators here consider it a reference to canonical prayer or worship generally

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Devoting religion entirely to God connotes sincere worship for His sake alone, a phrase often following the command to call upon Him.
rows.anchor: a phrase connoting sincere worship for the sake of God alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The analogy between original creation and resurrection shows that God's recognized creative power should dispel doubts about His ability to resurrect people.
rows.anchor: indicates the analogous nature of original creation and resurrection

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says people will be resurrected as they were born: barefoot, naked, and uncircumcised, alone and dependent on God.
rows.anchor: According to a ḥadīth, people will be resurrected in the same state as that in which they were born

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creation-resurrection parallel is echoed in 6:94 and elsewhere.
rows.anchor: See 6:94: And [God will say], “Now you have come unto Us alone, just as We created you the first time”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The account of Midian's destruction matches the account of the Thamūd, the people of Ṣāliḥ.
rows.anchor: The description of the destruction of the Midianites is identical to that of the Thamūd

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says God first sent Midian oppressive heat, then a cooling cloud that drew the people together before fire, a terrible cry, and an earthquake killed them.
rows.anchor: It is reported that when the people of Midian denied Shuʿayb, God first sent upon them such a terrible heat

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The earthquake erased Midian so completely that it seemed they had never lived there.
rows.anchor: The people of Midian were so thoroughly effaced by the earthquake that it was as though they had never dwelt there

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Against the disbelievers' claim that Shuʿayb's followers were losers, the passage declares the disbelievers deluded about true religion and destroyed.
rows.anchor: In response to the Midianite disbelievers’ description of Shuʿayb’s followers as the losers in v. 90

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The Israelites' division into communities around the earth is understood as the Jewish Diaspora.
rows.anchor: taken as a reference to the Diaspora, the existence of smaller communities of Jews in various locations throughout the world

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Righteousness remains possible for Jews who follow the Law and ritual prescribed in the Torah, including Sabbath observance emphasized by the Quran.
rows.anchor: a life of righteousness continues to be possible for those who follow Jewish Law and ritual as prescribed in the Torah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those described as otherwise are members of the Jewish community who do not follow the law.
rows.anchor: those who do not follow the law, although they continue to be members of this community

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Many commentators take the righteous Jews to mean Jews of the past, before Muhammad or even before Jesus.
rows.anchor: to pertain to the Jewish community of the past, before the coming of the Prophet Muhammad or even before the coming of Jesus

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another interpretation identifies the righteous Jews as those in Madinah who became Muslim.
rows.anchor: or else to the Jews in Madinah who became Muslim (R)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author questions those readings: the present tense points to the present and indefinite future, and to Jews who remain Jews.
rows.anchor: the verse is clearly in the present tense, indicating that it pertains to the present and the indefinite future

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good things are worldly provision and ease; evil things are forms of worldly adversity.
rows.anchor: The good things with which God tries them include worldly provision and ease; the evil things are various forms of worldly adversity

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Trials through good and bad fortune apply generally, not only to Jews, as 21:35 says explicitly.
rows.anchor: The trial by both good and bad fortune is not particular to the Jewish population, but is meant in a more general sense

words: إِنَّ ٱلَّذِينَ تَدْعُونَ مِن دُونِ ٱللَّهِ عِبَادٌ أَمْثَالُكُمْ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The challenge mocks idols and false deities as servants like their worshippers, belonging to God and subject to His sovereignty.
rows.anchor: mocking these false objects of worship as merely servants like themselves (v. 194), belonging to God and subject to His Sovereignty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The rhetorical questions stress that idols lack even human capacities, so it makes no sense to worship beings less capable than their worshippers.
rows.anchor: How, then, the questions imply, can one worship what is less capable than oneself?

words: قُلِ ٱدْعُوا۟ شُرَكَآءَكُمْ ثُمَّ كِيدُونِ فَلَا تُنظِرُونِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is told to challenge the idolaters to try their utmost to thwart God and the Prophet's mission.
rows.anchor: scheme against me, and grant me no respite, is that they try their best to thwart God and the mission of His Prophet

words: قُلِ ٱدْعُوا۟ شُرَكَآءَكُمْ ثُمَّ كِيدُونِ فَلَا تُنظِرُونِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Noah and Hūd issue identical or similar challenges to their peoples.
rows.anchor: This is identical or similar to statements made by Noah and Hūd to their disbelieving peoples

words: قُلِ ٱدْعُوا۟ شُرَكَآءَكُمْ ثُمَّ كِيدُونِ فَلَا تُنظِرُونِ
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The invitation to scheme recalls God's challenge to deniers; their plans cannot thwart Him, while His scheme remains firm despite granting respite.
rows.anchor: naught in the heavens or upon the earth can thwart God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's challenge displays complete confidence in God's succor and protection.
rows.anchor: demonstrates his utter confidence in God’s Succor and Protection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Walī is a Divine Name meaning Protector and also Friend.
rows.anchor: Protector translates Walī, a Divine Name invoked several times in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God specifically protects the righteous, as He protects the reverent and believers.
rows.anchor: God protects the righteous, specifically, as He protects the reverent

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who are with the Lord are understood to be angels.
rows.anchor: Those who are with thy Lord are understood to be the angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels are with God in the sense of nearness to His Mercy and Bounty.
rows.anchor: who are“with” Him in the sense of being near to His Mercy and Bounty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If pure and near angels do not disdain worship, imperfect and more distant humans have even less reason to refuse it.
rows.anchor: if the angels, with their spiritual purity and nearness to God, are not too arrogant to worship Him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse echoes 4:172, where Jesus and the angels would not disdain being God's servants or worshippers.
rows.anchor: where neither the messiah (Jesus) nor the angels would disdain to be a servant, or “worshipper,” of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels' constant praise and glorification of God is mentioned elsewhere in the Quran.
rows.anchor: constant praise and glorification of God is mentioned in several places in the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels' prostration is also mentioned at 16:49.
rows.anchor: That they prostrate unto Him is also mentioned in 16:49

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This is one of fifteen sajdah verses, marked in official Arabic Qurans to indicate physical prostration on recitation or hearing, though Islamic law does not require it.
rows.anchor: Muslims should physically prostrate upon reciting them or hearing them recited although this is not required by Islamic law

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators read desisting as ending enmity and hostility and embracing Islam.
rows.anchor: According to some commentators, this verse means that the disbelievers should stop their enmity and hostility and embrace Islam

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The final clause refers to God's established practice of destroying persistently corrupt and evil peoples.
rows.anchor: The last clause refers to God’s wont of destroying persistently corrupt and evil peoples

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wont can describe both what people do and what they undergo.
rows.anchor: Wont can also refer to both what people do and what they undergo

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith states that submission and repentance each cut off what came before.
rows.anchor: In a ḥadīth the Prophet said

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse does not explicitly require conversion to Islam; forgiveness can mean ending hostilities and resolving grievances.
rows.anchor: this verse says nothing explicitly about the disbelievers becoming Muslims, and “forgiveness” can refer to the cessation of hostilities

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The hypocrites are of their own kind and are not to be counted among believers.
rows.anchor: that is, they are not to be counted among the believers

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: One interpretation of clutching their hands shut is reluctance to participate in fighting.
rows.anchor: Clutching their hands shut refers to their reluctance to take part in fighting (Q)

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another interpretation is reluctance to spend and give in God's way.
rows.anchor: or to their reluctance to spend and give in the way of God (Ṭ)

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The phrase may encompass both refusing to fight and refusing to give.
rows.anchor: reluctance to spend and give in the way of God (Ṭ), or both

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: One reading says they abandoned devotion to God, so He abandoned them without guidance and compassion.
rows.anchor: They forgot God by abandoning devotion to Him (Ṭ), so He forgot them by abandoning them and leaving them without guidance and compassion

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another reading says they forgot God's remembrance and He acted toward them like one who forgot them.
rows.anchor: they forgot the remembrance of God, and God acted toward them like one who forgot them (IK)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The wording is echoed in the declaration that God forgets people as they forgot the meeting with Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: Today We forget you just as you forgot the meeting with this your Day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The hypocrites invert the Quran's usual ethic of enjoining right and forbidding wrong.
rows.anchor: Enjoining wrong, forbidding right is an inversion of the usual command in the Quran to enjoin right and forbid wrong

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The description of believers mirrors the preceding description of hypocrites.
rows.anchor: This verse in a sense mirrors the description of the hypocrites in v. 67

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The discussion of enjoining right and forbidding wrong is cross-referenced to 3:104.
rows.anchor: On enjoining right and forbidding wrong, see 3:104c

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Protectors of one another also means friends or allies of one another.
rows.anchor: Protectors of one another also means friends or allies of one another

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse gives women the same spiritual and social obligations as men, including moral authority and protection.
rows.anchor: it places upon them the same spiritual and social obligations placed on men, including moral authority and protection

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Like other descriptions of hypocrites in this sūrah, these verses are understood generally.
rows.anchor: As with other descriptions of the hypocrites in this sūrah, these verses are understood in a general sense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some commentators connect the passage with Thaʿlabah ibn Ḥāṭib, who promised charity if wealthy, prospered after receiving spoils, moved away, gradually stopped congregational and Friday prayers, then refused zakāh as jizyah; the Prophet rebuked him.
rows.anchor: some commentators also connect them with a certain Thaʿlabah ibn Ḥāṭib

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sirr can mean either a secret itself or the hidden or mysterious aspect of something.
rows.anchor: can mean both the thing kept secret as well as the aspect of a thing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Najwā means conversation among confidants; here it refers to hypocrites' insults about the Prophet and believers.
rows.anchor: referring to conversations held between confidants, in this case referring to the insults the hypocrites exchange with one another about the Prophet and the believers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unseen consists of real things absent from present sensory perception or belonging to another time or state of being.
rows.anchor: things that are real but absent from sensory perception in the present moment or absent because they will occur or have occurred at a different moment in time or state of being

rows.speaker: Aj
rows.claim: Virtuous spiritual people contrast with hypocrites: they accept God's provision and worship and remember Him unseen; their private discourse is worship rather than mockery.
rows.anchor: virtuous and spiritual persons are the reverse of hypocrites; they are satisfied with what God gives them and worship and remember God when no one can see

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report connects the verse with the repentant men of 9:102: after they offered their wealth, the Prophet initially said he had not been commanded to accept it; revelation then directed them to give a third as expiation.
rows.anchor: It is said that this verse was revealed in connection with the repentant men of v. 102

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some Arabian tribes after the Prophet's death used this interpretation to argue that alms were owed only to him personally and refused to give them to Abū Bakr.
rows.anchor: those Arabian tribes who believed that alms were only owed to the Prophet personally for him to distribute

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the first interpretation, the charitable offering is expiation charity.
rows.anchor: According to this interpretation, the charitable offering refers to the charity of expiation

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The other main opinion takes the offering as institutional obligatory alms, usually called zakāh.
rows.anchor: this verse refers to the institutional alms

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse cannot restrict obligatory alms to payments made directly to the Prophet, since other verses specify recipients such as the poor, indigent, beggar, and deprived.
rows.anchor: This verse could not, it is argued, be the basis for restricting obligatory alms to those given directly to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quran also describes messengers as purifying people, often together with teaching the Book and imparting knowledge.
rows.anchor: The purification of a people by a messenger is also mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving charity purifies a person from the defilement of sin and disobedience to God.
rows.anchor: The giving of charity purifies one from the defilement of sin and disobedience to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The commentary refers the meaning of blessings to its discussions at 2:3, 9:99, and 33:56.
rows.anchor: On the meaning of the blessings

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: It is said that the Prophet would pray, O God, bless them, when people brought charity for distribution to the community.
rows.anchor: when someone brought charity to the Prophet for distribution to the community, he would pray, “O God, bless them

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: The Prophet's blessings comfort people because hearing his prayers makes them glad and God's response brings peace to their hearts.
rows.anchor: when people heard the Prophet’s prayers, they became glad and, as a result of God’s Response to his prayers, found peace in their hearts

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Another explanation is that the Prophet's blessings are a mercy for the people.
rows.anchor: his blessings were a mercy for them

rows.speaker: commentators
rows.claim: Many hold that this form of blessing is restricted to the Prophet: Muslims invoke blessings only on him, and only he may bless others.
rows.anchor: Many say that the act of blessing in this particular way is reserved only for the Prophet

rows.speaker: al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī
rows.claim: Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī reject restricting this form of blessing to the Prophet because he is an exemplar for all actions.
rows.anchor: Al-Rāzī and al-Qurṭubī, however, are of the opinion that there is no reason why this particular form of invoking blessings should be restricted to the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muslims invoke blessings and peace upon Muhammad in prayer and when his name is mentioned, but invoke only peace for other prophets.
rows.anchor: Muslims invoke blessings and peace upon the Prophet Muhammad in prayers and also when his name is mentioned, while only peace is invoked in the case of other prophets
